Mains are a choice of two steaks, such as strip loin and filet, or the signature sirloin with a crisp crust, eaten with rice and miso soup. tokyo_yakiuo_ishikawa_mitsukoshi.notes: [Seafood · fish grilled like yakiniku] A 24-seat restaurant on the 12th floor of the Ginza Mitsukoshi annex (13 at the counter, 9 in a private counter room), opened in 2025. It serves 'yaki-uo', a fish version of yakiniku developed over eight years by the founder of Tsukiji Aozora. Premium cuts are grilled in front of you, such as fatty tuna billed as 'special kalbi', with house condiments and sauces. 2026 diners started with the brain, then had fresh mehikari, a yukhoe-like dish and a sukiyaki-style course (just under ¥4,000 plus ¥400 service). The ladies' lunch adds rice with refills, cold noodles and dessert. The grill staff are chatty. Many guests are visitors from Hong Kong and Singapore. A touch salty, and slow at times.

Some find the portions small for the price. Cashless only.

tokyo_hakone_akatsukian_ginza_mitsukoshi.notes: [Soba · Hakone's Akatsuki An on the Mitsukoshi restaurant floor] The Ginza Mitsukoshi branch, since 2010, of the Hakone soba house. Buckwheat is stone-milled in-house every day and the noodles are made by hand in view; the head chef, Ozaki, learned directly from soba master Kunihiro Takahashi. The dipping sauce blends several Makurazaki katsuobushi, with different broths for hot and cold soba. The striking dish is a smooth, firm, jet-black charcoal soba. Tororo zaru (¥1,800 in 2026) and tender duck tsukesoba are regulars' picks. Open straight through the afternoon, it is handy for a 4 pm lunch, and families and overseas visitors fill the 34 seats (six counter, six semi-private). Kind, attentive staff.

Drinks are served from lunchtime, and following the shop on Instagram earns a free drink, softening prices regulars call on the high side. Queues move quickly. Wheelchair accessible; allergy information available.

tokyo_varmen_midtown_hibiya.notes: [Bistro · seafood and wine above Hibiya Park] Open since 2018 on the second floor of Tokyo Midtown Hibiya, a collaboration between Daikanyama's hard-to-book seafood bistro Ata (Michelin-listed ten years running, per the listing) and Niigata's CAVE DOCCI winery. Lunch is great value: ¥1,800–2,000 sets with a shared salad platter (with couscous) and a choice of pasta (such as liver bolognese), gratin or curry. There are 38 seats at the entrance bar, counter, tables and a terrace over Hibiya Park, handy before the Hibiya theatres. Walk-ins sometimes get in at Saturday noon.

tokyo_pais_vasco_ginza.notes: [Spanish · Basque food in a red-brick Ginza 7-chōme alley house] A three-storey red-brick house at the end of a narrow alley, open since 2012: a bar on the ground floor and tables on the two floors above, 40 seats in all. Txakoli is poured from height in the Basque way, alongside 50+ Spanish wines (mostly by the bottle). Staff with Dalí moustaches set the mood. Open to 2 am on weekdays; charge ¥400; smoking only at the entrance terrace.

A bit pricey; English menu; dinner service charge 10%.

tokyo_ginza_sushiko_honten.notes: [Sushi · Ginza's Edomae house since 1885] Founded in 1885 and now run by the fourth-generation owner 杉山衛 (Sugiyama), president since 1992, who is known for pioneering sushi with wine. Sugiyama's line is that the Ginza sushi counter is "a place for courtship". There are 40 seats: a white-wood counter of 24 (some upstairs) and three tatami rooms. The site highlights tuna, hoshi-garei (spotted flounder), shinko, kohada and sweet shrimp; reviewers single out an unusual shima-aji and shiitake nigiri and gentle classic rice. The owner chats warmly at the counter, easing the formality, and the wine pairing wins converts. It's also a stop for fans of the writer Ikenami Shōtarō. Dinner runs about ¥20,000–40,000. The group also has Marunouchi Building and Kōjun Building shops.

chef_bio.background: Fourth-generation president since 1992 (official site). Three shops: Ginza honten, Marunouchi Building, Kōjun Building (official site).
chef_bio.philosophy: "Tradition is not something to be preserved, but something to be created" (Tabelog listing).

A 16-visit regular loves it; one diner found the fried shrimp heads greasy. Card only; 5% service charge.

tokyo_kinniku_shokudo_ginza_corridor.notes: [Health food · the protein canteen on Corridor-gai] A 44-seat branch of the Kinniku Shokudō ("Muscle Canteen") chain, open since 2018 up a flight of stairs on Ginza Corridor-gai. Every item lists calories and protein-fat-carb numbers, and meals start with a small cup of protein shake. The signatures are a lean-beef hamburg and a surprisingly moist 200 g chicken-breast steak, plus skinless grilled chicken, domestic beef steaks, salmon and limited red-meat platters, with craft beer or wine. One dieting regular credits it with a 10 kg loss; another diner called the value merely average for Ginza. Seat-only bookings are capped at 90 minutes when busy; no cover charge.

The house beef is Arita wagyu, which the listing says won gold at the 2025 World Steak Challenge. The famous dish is a limited green-onion-wrapped tongue, bundled like an inari pouch and served with dashi; there's also offal and cold noodles, and à la carte diners pick their meat from packed portions. A gentle charcoal fire means no rushing. Courses with all-you-can-drink keep it reasonable, and ask about rare sake off the menu. The booking form asks about allergies.

tokyo_mutsukari_ginza.notes: [Japanese · Akiyama's "super kappō" a minute from Ginza crossing] Open since 2004, a Japanese restaurant over two floors (46 seats), reached along a stone-paved passage scented with incense. The 9-seat counter faces an open kitchen where chef Yoshihisa Akiyama cooks what the listing calls "new Edomae Tokyo style". The seasonal omakase might run sesame tofu, conger eel, somen with sea urchin and junsai, charcoal-grilled ayu, beef shabu wrapped round a thick yuba roll, and mushroom or corn rice with red miso soup. It ends with the famous shaved ice (pumpkin in autumn). The signature vegetable dish is a nikogori terrine of ten vegetables. A sake sommelier pairs drinks; service is attentive without hovering. Tabelog Award Bronze 2017 and 2018; dinner ¥20,000–40,000; no under-12s.

It serves traditional dishes of the kind Paris bistros have cooked for a century, with about 200 wines, mostly French, drawn from a 40,000-bottle stock, and free-flow Champagne plans. The prix-fixe lets you pick a starter, main and dessert; regulars rave about the duck, recommended mussels, a jelly and a chocolate dessert. It's good value for Ginza (lunch about ¥4,000–5,000, dinner ¥6,000–10,000), though one table waited long between courses and spent three hours. Walk-ins are sometimes possible at Saturday lunch.

tokyo_ginza_espero_spanish.notes: [Spanish · six decades of paella a minute from Ginza crossing] A 50-seat basement Spanish restaurant that has served Ginza for over 60 years and was renovated in 2020. At night, try tomato and anchovy salad, mushroom ajillo, stuffed squid with a standout sea-urchin sauce and squid-ink paella. Queues at weekday lunch; some find the salad and tortilla salty.

The autumn picks are a chestnut Mont Blanc and an apple chiboust with a crisp caramelised top. tokyo_ueno_seiyoken_matsuya_ginza.notes: [Yōshoku · Ueno Seiyōken on the Matsuya restaurant floor] The Ginza branch of Ueno Seiyōken, the 1872 pioneer of Western cooking in Japan, on Matsuya's eighth floor: a small entrance opening onto 50 spacious, comfortable seats. The draw is the classic beef hamburg in a refined demi-glace, thick and coarse-ground, with broccoli, carrot and potato. Crab cream croquettes and beef stew are the other standards; one regular found the croquette batter thick. Family-friendly, with a kids' menu, baby chairs and room for strollers. One diner found online slots that couldn't actually be booked. Lunch about ¥2,000–3,000.

tokyo_rogovski_ginza.notes: [Russian · Japan's first Russian restaurant, now 75] Founded in 1951 and billed as Japan's first Russian restaurant, Rogovski celebrates its 75th year on the seventh floor of EXIT MELSA at Ginza 5-chōme crossing (76 seats; Tabelog dates this listing from 2015). It serves court-style Russian dishes alongside Ukrainian, Georgian and Uzbek specialities, with wines from Georgia, Moldova, Romania and Bulgaria. The Katyusha lunch course opens with six zakuski (pickled herring, beet vinaigrette salad, marinated wild mushrooms), then freshly fried pirozhki (meat or vegetable), borscht with red wine, and a main such as beef stroganoff or mushroom-and-chicken tsubo-yaki, with Russian tea. Portions are big. Important for allergies: it says it cannot accommodate dairy, egg, wheat, pork, mushroom or green-onion allergies.

tokyo_echigoya_yasokichi_ginza.notes: [Izakaya · charcoal-grilled himono by Higashi-Ginza] A 70-seat old-style house, long and narrow like an eel's bed, with counter, tatami and sunken seating, built around dried fish from across Japan and fresh seafood from its own Tsukiji wholesale shop. Fish is charcoal-grilled the "strong fire, distant heat" way, crisp skin over just-cooked flesh. Salmon harasu and half a shima-hokke are ¥890 each, set meals start at ¥790, and a two-person sashimi platter is ¥790. Fish, rice and miso soup can be ordered separately any time. Evenings bring an omakase of five fish skewers and seasonal sake. Lunch queues are long and tables may be shared; one diner found the miso soup lukewarm. Two-hour limit.

tokyo_kamon_imperial_hotel.notes: [Teppanyaki · Imperial Hotel's 17th-floor teppan] The Imperial Hotel Tokyo's teppanyaki on the 17th floor of the main building, with city views. It stands where the French restaurant Fontainebleau served three decades ago, per a reviewer who once worked at the hotel. Chefs grill for each party at the counter: Ise lobster, black abalone, wagyu fillet (Miyagi wagyu on one October visit) and vegetables, finishing with garlic rice. Dessert is served in a separate room so it's away from the smell of the grill. It's a celebration place: one couple who dined here on their wedding day came back for their daughter's birthday. Special courses run ¥40,000–50,000 at dinner, lunch from about ¥15,000; 15% service charge.

The buckwheat is stone-ground, and seasonal fish and vegetable tempura is fried light in sesame oil. Adults come to drink first, ordering tempura, seasonal snacks such as returning bonito, ginkgo and ayu, and shochu cut with soba-yu, then finish with zaru soba. Warm soba in a well-made broth and a crisp ten-don suit solo lunches. The room is calm and the crowd mostly older; Ginza prices. The Matsuya Ginza 8F branch is listed separately.

It serves thin, smooth, chewy Inaniwa noodles. Seiro ni-aji (¥1,400 in October 2026) comes with two dips, soy and a rich sesame miso; there's also tempura seiro with plump shrimp, tempura udon, a sweet-glazed ten-don, chicken tempura seiro and butter chicken curry. Many overseas visitors; orders by QR code; prices are high for udon.

Expect queues: one weekday lunch took two hours from 11:00, and evening tickets go out from 4 pm, with about ten people waiting before then. Premium and omakase nigiri come piece by piece; extras such as daimyō mackerel and off-menu grilled squid tentacles with onion and butter can be ordered. Around ¥3,000–6,000 a head. tokyo_ginza_ukaitei.notes: [Teppanyaki · Ukai-tei on Miyuki-dōri] Ginza's Ukai-tei, entered through a door bearing a Jean-Michel Folon sculpture into a room of century-old zelkova beams mixing Japanese architecture and Western art, with a 22-seat counter and nine semi-private rooms (94 seats). Chefs cook Ukai-selected beef in front of you, along with abalone (one diner's best of the meal) and seasonal courses. Autumn brought sea bream en croûte, clam soup, chestnut soup and a chestnut Mont Blanc, with extra matsutake to order; earlier menus ran black-wagyu tartare and strip loin with black pepper sauce. Wine and sake pairings are offered. Tabelog Award Bronze 2017–2020. Lunch about ¥15,000–20,000. Strict cancellation fees; service charge rises from 13% to 15% on 1 December 2026.

tokyo_ginza_miyazawa_kissa.notes: [Kissa · Miyazawa, Ginza's late-night sandwich café, relocated] Founded in 1983 in Ginza 8-chōme, Miyazawa was a Showa-era kissa known for sandwiches and late-night delivery. In 2026 it moved a short walk toward Shimbashi into a bright, stylish space (Tabelog's opening date is 1 October; one reviewer says January), with 30-plus table seats, a big counter with power outlets and friendly staff. The signatures are the egg sandwich and a tuna-egg-cucumber mixed sandwich (¥1,300, takeaway too), plus omurice and Napolitan. Lunch brings limited sandwiches and sets with a drink, such as pork ginger at ¥1,500. Hot coffee is ¥800. It's open until 4 am on weeknights; staff ask about smoking when you enter.

tokyo_ginza_ashibi_soba.notes: [Soba · ju-wari soba and sake on Sukiya-dōri] A soba-and-sake restaurant on the second floor along Sukiya-dōri in Ginza 6-chōme, with a white-wood counter, tables and private rooms; reviewers compare it to a fine ryōtei. The owner makes ju-wari soba from Hitachi Aki buckwheat (rooted in a native strain from the old Kanasagō village), stone-milled fine with the inner husk to keep its aroma and sweetness. Evenings run to Japanese courses and plentiful soba-house appetisers, such as nori, miso-cured cream cheese, salted fish, dried squid, karasumi, tamagoyaki and homemade satsuma-age. Finish with soba, perhaps under a jumbo prawn tempura, and soba-yu cut with Ashibi shochu. Reviewers praise the owner's hospitality. On weekdays 15:30–18:00 there's a lower-priced ten-don and ju-wari soba deal. Dinner ¥10,000–20,000.
